title: Records (value equality and with-expressions)
hook: A record is a type whose main job is holding data — not behavior or identity. C# generates value equality, a readable `ToString`, and `with`-expressions so you can copy and tweak without mutating the original.

blocks.text: A **record** is a reference type (`record` or `record class`) or value type (`record struct`) optimized for immutable data. Two record instances compare **equal by value** — same type, same member values — even if they are different objects on the heap. Positional syntax (`record AuthToken(string Subject, string Issuer)`) generates a primary constructor, init-only properties, `Deconstruct`, and a formatted `ToString`.

entries.plainDefinition: A reference type with value equality. Lives on the heap but compares by member values, not identity.
A value type with value equality. Copies on assignment like any struct.
entries.example: `readonly record struct CacheKey(string Tenant, string Id);`

entries.plainDefinition: Creates a new record instance by copying the original and overlaying named properties. Does not mutate.
A record declared with parameters in parentheses. The compiler generates constructor, properties, equality, and Deconstruct.

blocks.text: Auth tokens, Redis Data Transfer Objects (DTOs), and API response shapes are pure data — they do not need identity or virtual dispatch. Records give you concise syntax and correct equality out of the box. Your SQS worker host, on the other hand, has behavior and lifetime — that stays a class. Using a record where you need a service, or a class where you need value equality, leads to subtle bugs in dictionaries and tests.

blocks.title: with does not mutate
blocks.body: `var refreshed = token with { ExpiresAt = newTime }` creates a new instance. The original `token` is unchanged. This is how you refresh an expiry without touching the copy sitting in a cache.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Declare a positional record
items.body: `record AuthToken(string Subject, string Issuer, DateTimeOffset ExpiresAt);` — the compiler generates constructor, init properties, equality, `ToString`, and `Deconstruct`.

items.title: Create instances
items.body: `new AuthToken("user-9", "https://auth.example", expiry)` or use the generated constructor.

items.title: Compare by value
items.body: Two records with the same type and same property values return true from `Equals`, even if they are different heap objects.

items.title: Copy with changes using with
items.body: `token with { ExpiresAt = newExpiry }` produces a new record. The original is untouched.

snippet.label: Auth token and Redis DTO records
snippet.explanation: Line 1: positional record class with one custom method. Line 6: readonly record struct for cache metadata. Line 10: `with` creates a copy with a new expiry. Lines 12–13: value equality compares all members; `Subject` matches but the records are not equal overall.

snippet.label: Deconstruct and formatted ToString
snippet.explanation: Line 1: positional record — compiler generates members. Line 6: `ToString` prints all properties in a readable format. Line 10: `Deconstruct` lets you unpack into variables — useful in pattern matching (module 11).

snippet.label: When NOT to use a record
snippet.explanation: Line 2: `Attempt` has identity (`Id`) and mutable `Score` — a class with reference equality is appropriate. Line 10: a record with `set` accessors is legal but you lose the safe-to-use-as-dictionary-key property. Prefer init-only or positional records for DTOs.

blocks.title: Records across languages
rows: No built-in; `===` is reference equality for objects

blocks.title: Using a mutable record as a dictionary key
blocks.body: If any property has a `set` accessor and someone mutates it after inserting into a `Dictionary`, the entry becomes unreachable. Records help only when they stay immutable. Use `init` or positional syntax.

blocks.title: Expecting record struct inheritance
blocks.body: `record struct` cannot inherit from another `record struct` or class. Only `record class` supports inheritance between records. Plan your type hierarchy accordingly.

blocks.text: The compiler synthesizes `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `==`, `!=`, and `IEquatable<T>` for records using every **included** member — positional parameters, init properties, and base record properties in an inheritance chain. Two `AuthToken` instances on different heap addresses compare equal when every included member matches; that is why records work as dictionary keys and test fixtures without hand-written equality. `with`-expressions perform a **nondestructive copy**: the compiler generates a clone method that copies all included members and overlays the named changes, preserving the runtime type in hierarchies (`derived with { X = 1 }` stays `Derived`). `record struct` avoids a heap allocation for small bundles like cache keys but still gets synthesized equality — use `readonly record struct` to prevent accidental mutation. How to prove it in production: unit test `Assert.Equal(token1, token2)` across two `new` instances with identical claims; put the same record in a `Dictionary` and look up with a different instance — a miss means equality or hashing broke.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Heap allocation; not for identity entities
Cannot inherit; copies on every pass-by-value
Full control over identity vs value semantics
Easy to break the Equals/GetHashCode pair
Dictionary key safety lost; equality can change after insert
Base members included in synthesized equality
with and equality include base properties — surprises if base is large

snippet.label: Record equality in a dictionary — the production proof
snippet.explanation: Line 1: compiler generates matching Equals and GetHashCode from all positional members. Lines 4–6: insert with one instance. Lines 9–10: a second `new` with identical values finds the entry — value equality, not reference. Lines 13–14: `with` changes `ExpiresAt`, so the refreshed token is a different key. This is the behavior Redis DTOs and auth tokens rely on in tests and caches.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying records are just classes with less syntax — they synthesize equality, hashing, with, Deconstruct, and ToString. Claiming `with` mutates the original — it creates a new instance. Using a record for an entity with database identity (`Attempt` with mutable Score) — reference equality on a class is the right model. Putting a mutable record (with `set`) in a Dictionary — mutation after insert orphans the entry. Strong answer: record for immutable DTOs with value equality; class for identity entities; readonly record struct for small cache keys; equality is compiler-generated and must stay paired with hashing.

interviewTakeaways: record class: heap object with compiler-synthesized value equality; record struct: stack copy with the same equality generation.
Use records for immutable DTOs (auth tokens, Redis shapes); use classes when identity and mutable state matter (Attempt with Id).
In production, two `new AuthToken(...)` instances with identical claims must find the same Dictionary slot — if not, equality generation was broken or the record was mutated.

60s: Records synthesize Equals, GetHashCode, with, Deconstruct, and ToString. Value equality across different heap objects. with is nondestructive copy. record struct for small cache keys without heap allocation. Never use mutable set accessors on dictionary keys.
Follow-up: how does record inheritance include base properties in synthesized equality?
commonPitfalls: Saying with mutates the original — that gets rejected because with always returns a new instance.
Strong answer: records generate a consistent Equals/GetHashCode pair; use them for immutable DTOs, not identity entities with mutable state.
Using a mutable record (set accessors) as a dictionary key — mutation after insert changes the hash and orphans the entry.
Expecting record struct to support inheritance — only record class inherits, and base members participate in equality.
